title: eCommerce customer experience: What influences the reorder
summary: eCommerce customer experience doesn’t end at checkout. See the moments that decide the reorder, how to improve each one, and how to measure what’s working.
body_markdown:
eCommerce customer experience (CX) is the sum of every interaction a customer has with an online store, from how they discover a product through checkout, delivery, support, and the decision to buy again.


Most eCommerce experience work focuses on the parts of the journey that happen on your website, while many repeat-purchase decisions are made elsewhere. The website is the obvious place to start, as product pages and checkout flows are within your control and easy to test and improve. But things that influence a customer’s decision to return are less predictable and less visible, like what happens when a customer refreshes a tracking page for an order that’s a day late, or is trying to send something back.


Below, we’ll walk through the moments that shape the experience and how to improve each one, beginning with the changes with quick paybacks. We’ll also look at what happens during the delivery window, across industries, and how to tell whether any changes to the process are impactful.


**TL;DR**


- eCommerce customer experience (CX) is the sum of every interaction a customer has with an online store, from how they discover a product through checkout, delivery, support, and the decision to buy again.
- Many repeat purchase decisions are influenced by moments when the customer isn’t on your website, like while they’re waiting for their order to arrive.
- Start with the improvements that will provide the largest benefit for the least amount of effort, such as proactively answering your most-asked support question and sending order status updates before customers ask.
- Delivery windows look different across industries, and can stretch from just a few minutes to several weeks. The length shapes what customers need to hear.
- Name the denominator for every rate you measure, and use a holdout group to prove that any changes are impactful.


## What is eCommerce customer experience?


Customer experience in eCommerce runs across marketing, merchandising, eCommerce, fulfillment, and support, so no single team owns it. Marketing controls only part of the picture, which is often why efforts to improve customer experience for eCommerce stall. Each team works on its own piece separately, while the customer experiences them all as one.


eCommerce customer experience has five moments: discovery, evaluation, checkout, the wait, and the return or reorder decision, and here’s who typically owns them.


- **Marketing** focuses on getting people to the site in the first place, then winning them back after delivery with reorder messages and loyalty programs
- **Merchandising** focuses on discovery and evaluation, meaning site search, navigation, and the product content shoppers use to decide
- **eCommerce** focuses on the website checkout experience, making sure the path from cart to confirmation is quick and there are no surprises
- **Fulfillment** focuses on the wait, from order confirmation to delivery, plus the logistics side of returns
- **Support** focuses on picking up the questions the experience didn’t answer, especially “where’s my order?” and running returns.


Personalization improves the experience by deciding what each customer sees and receives, but tends to be handled in various ways by different teams, and indicates why marketing should remain involved post-purchase.


## The five moments that shape the product experience in eCommerce


Customers can drift away at any point, and the reason tends to change as they go. On your site, it’s usually because they can’t find what they’re after, or a cost they weren’t expecting pops up at checkout. After placing an order, they wonder why they’ve heard nothing about their delivery. Or, a return suddenly becomes a hassle. Figure out where you’re losing people, and you’ll know which team needs to step in.


### Discovery


When someone lands on your site, they’re looking for something worth wanting, and they won’t look for long. Product discovery relies on site search that understands what people type and navigation that matches how they think about your range. It falls apart when search stumbles over a misspelling or an everyday word, or when the filters leave out the one detail a shopper cares about. Merchandising and the eCommerce team usually own this moment, while marketing looks after how people find you in the first place.


### Evaluation


Once they’ve found something, shoppers want to answer their own questions without leaving the page. Will it fit? When will it turn up? If the product content is thin or the reviews are buried, every unanswered question becomes a reason to open another tab and look elsewhere. Product content tends to sit with merchandising, while reviews often land with marketing or support.


### Checkout


By checkout, the customer has made up their mind, and all they want is the total they were expecting. Checkout friction usually shows up as a surprise at the last step, like a delivery charge nobody mentioned earlier or being made to create an account. That’s often where cart abandonment happens. The eCommerce team owns the checkout flow, though delivery pricing is often decided somewhere else in the business.


### The wait


The wait starts with the order confirmation and ends when the package arrives, and it’s usually the longest stretch of the whole experience. For a few days, sometimes longer, your customer has paid and has nothing to show for it but an order number. What they want is simple enough. They want to know where their order is and when it’ll arrive, without chasing it.


This is where things often slip. Order status updates stop after the confirmation email, or a delay goes unmentioned until the customer spots it themselves. A tracking link that drops them on a carrier page with no trace of your brand doesn’t help much either. Each of those gaps turns “where’s my order?” into a support ticket, when a quick update could have answered it first.


Fulfillment and operations handle the logistics, and the carrier controls a lot of what the customer actually sees. Marketing tends to step away after the order confirmation, which is a shame, because this is when your customer has every reason to pay attention.


### The return or reorder decision


Once the package arrives, your customer works out whether this was a one-off purchase. If something’s not right, the returns experience is influential. Customers want a simple way to send it back and a refund that turns up when you say it will. A return that feels like a battle usually ends the relationship, while an easy one can leave them happy to give you another chance.


If the product *is* right, it all comes down to your timing for the next message. A “buy again” message sent minutes after the order arrives reaches them before they’ve even tried out what they bought. The post-purchase moment can directly move repeat purchase rate, so it’s important to get it right.


It’s also the moment with the most hands on it. Support and operations run returns, while marketing or the lifecycle team owns loyalty programs and reorder messages. If those teams aren’t talking, a customer halfway through a return can still get an email inviting them to buy again.

## How to improve the eCommerce customer experience online, in order of return


If you’re working out how to improve customer experience online, start at the top of this list. These online store customer experience improvement strategies are ranked, starting with the biggest benefit for the least effort. The top ones fix problems your customers are already raising, using first-party data you almost certainly have, like support tickets and order events. Further down, more of your systems will need to talk to each other, which takes longer but goes deeper into influencing repeat purchases. Each fix explains how the change works and how to tell whether it’s working, so you can prove one before moving on to the next.


### 1. Answer the question your customers ask most


Go through your support tickets, find the question that comes up most often, and answer it before anyone needs to ask, on the product page or in the order confirmation. If it’s working, contacts about that topic fall as a share of orders placed.


### 2. Send order status updates before customers ask


Trigger a message when an order ships and again if it’s delayed, on whichever channel each customer is most likely to see. You’ll know it’s working when “where’s my order?” contacts per hundred orders begin to drop.


### 3. Recover the cart with what was in it


A cart reminder that shows the exact item and price someone left behind gives them a concrete reason to come back, and[abandoned cart emails](https://www.braze.com/resources/articles/abandoned-cart-email) work best when you also have the option to follow up on other channels. Measure the share of abandoned carts that become orders within your recovery window, compared with a holdout group that gets no reminder.


### 4. Show the returns policy before checkout


Putting the returns window and cost on product pages and at checkout removes a reason to hesitate, especially for first-time buyers. Look for an increase in the percentage of first-time visitors who complete a purchase, and keep an eye on the total number of returns compared to total orders.


### 5. Stop your messages from contradicting each other


Connect return and delivery status to your cross-channel messaging, so a customer with an open return or a late order is held back from promotions and “buy again” emails until it’s resolved. If you stop sending automated or irrelevant marketing messages to customers with an open issue, your unsubscribe and complaint rates should drop.


### 6. Turn back-in-stock and price-drop signals into messages


When an item a customer viewed or saved comes back in stock or drops in price, a message triggered by that change brings them back to something they’ve already shown interest in, a simple form of[real-time personalization](https://www.braze.com/resources/articles/real-time-personalization) . Compare conversion among customers who got the alert with those who were eligible but held out.


### 7. Time the next ask from delivery instead of purchase


Starting post-purchase messages like reorder and review requests from the delivery date, and spacing them around how long the product takes to use, means they arrive once the customer can judge what they bought, which is the heart of most[customer retention strategies](https://www.braze.com/resources/articles/customer-retention-strategies) . Repeat purchase rate over a set period, compared with customers still on the old timing, shows whether the change paid off.


### 8. Personalize once the basics are in place


By tailoring products and offers to individual customers,[eCommerce personalization](https://www.braze.com/resources/articles/ecommerce-personalization-guide) boosts your other optimizations because it ensures you are maximizing the value of a user experience that already works. Compare the share of recipients who buy, or revenue per customer, for personalized messages against a control group receiving the standard version.


## What the delivery window looks like in four industries


The window after a customer commits looks different across industries. The length of that window determines what the customer needs to hear from you, and when.


### eCommerce: an order in transit


For an[online retailer](https://www.braze.com/solutions/retail-and-ecommerce) , the delivery window runs from dispatch to doorstep, which generally takes a few days. Mostly, the customer wants to know that nothing has gone wrong, so an update at each step helps: when it shipped, any changes along its delivery path, and an alert on the morning it will arrive. Missed updates or radio silence can send someone to support.


### On-demand: a wait measured in minutes


When someone orders dinner or books a ride, the wait might be 20 minutes, and they’ll check their phone for updates. That status update is part of what they’re paying for, so live tracking and an accurate arrival time matter almost as much as the order itself. If the estimate keeps slipping, they’ll remember the next time they’re deciding whether to place an order, so the reorder decision arrives almost as soon as the food does.


### Travel: a wait measured in weeks


Trips are often booked weeks or months in advance, which is a long period for the customer to wonder whether everything’s in order. Between booking and departure, offering reassurance is key to the experience. That might be sending confirmations or an early warning about a schedule change. Long silences can leave a traveler second-guessing their booking while they still have time to cancel.


### Subscriptions and streaming: the days before a renewal


Subscriptions don’t have a delivery window per se, but they do have a moment that works similarly, which is the immediate period of time before the customer is charged next. That stretch of days is when a customer decides whether the service is still worth paying for, a version of the return or reorder decision. Sending them a reminder that the renewal is coming, along with what’s new since last time, gives them a reason to stay and spares them a surprise on their statement. It’s a stage to plan for within your[customer lifecycle management](https://www.braze.com/resources/articles/customer-lifecycle-management) .


## How to measure eCommerce customer experience


When measuring customer experience, it helps to know which type of metric you’re looking at, because each answers a different question. For every rate, name the denominator, meaning the number it’s divided by. An eCommerce conversion rate, for example, can be divided by sessions, unique visitors, or addressable customers, and each gives a very different result for the same store. Average eCommerce conversion tends to sit between[2% and 4% of visitors](https://marketing.dynamicyield.com/benchmarks/conversion-rate/) , though it varies widely by industry, and a rate based on sessions won’t compare directly with one based on visitors.


### Outcome measures


Outcome measures tell you whether the business is better off, so these matter most. Repeat purchase rate is the share of customers who bought more than once in a period, with all customers who bought in that period as the denominator. Revenue per customer uses unique customers as its denominator. Both move slowly, so they’re better for judging long-term progress than any single change.


### Behavioral measures


Behavioral measures track what customers do, and because they react quickly, they’re often the first sign that something is working. Support contact rate divides support contacts by orders. Time to first value is how long it takes a new customer to get something useful from what they bought.


### Stated measures


CSAT, NPS, and other survey scores capture what customers tell you, and NPS measures those who are likely to promote your brand. They’re useful for understanding why something is happening, and a[customer experience platform](https://www.braze.com/resources/articles/customer-experience-platform) can connect that feedback to customer actions. These scores are also the most often over-read. A score that moves after a change isn’t evidence on its own, since who answered can shift too. For survey scores, the denominator is either respondents or everyone surveyed, so define which.


Real evidence comes from a holdout, a random group of eligible customers kept on the old experience. If an outcome or behavioral measure improves for everyone else compared with that group, the change made the difference.

## How Braze supports eCommerce customer experience


Braze is a customer engagement platform. It works alongside your commerce platform, order management system, and support desk by taking the signals those systems produce and using them to shape the message each customer receives next.


Say a shopper finds a jacket they like, but it’s out of stock in their size. If your stock levels already sit in your cloud data warehouse, **warehouse-native, zero-copy data** means Braze can trigger a back-in-stock alert straight from there, without duplicating catalog or order data. The alert brings them back into discovery with something they already wanted.


When they return, their history is already recorded on **a unified customer profile** in the[Braze Data Platform](https://www.braze.com/product/braze-data-platform) . The jacket they saved and the size guide they opened during evaluation sit alongside the messages they’ve already received, so the next message follows on from what they looked at.


Once they order, the conversation moves off your site. **Native execution across email, push, in-app, web, SMS, and WhatsApp** all run through the same platform during the delivery window. A push goes out when the jacket ships, and an SMS follows if the delivery slips, all as part of one journey with a single set of frequency rules. Running[cross-channel messaging](https://www.braze.com/product/cross-channel-messaging) from one place keeps updates consistent, no matter which channel they arrive on.


[BrazeAI™](https://www.braze.com/product/brazeai) helps each of those messages land.
